findings.title: Duplicate null-check bug: rawTokenId is never validated
findings.body: In the AccessTokenContext constructor, line 73 reads `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");` which checks `grantType` twice (once on line 72) instead of checking `rawTokenId`. As a result, a null `rawTokenId` is silently accepted. Later, `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId()` concatenates `':' + tokenContext.getRawTokenId()`, so a null rawTokenId would simply produce the literal string "null" appended to the token id instead of failing fast, risking malformed/duplicate access-token IDs rather than an early, clear error.

findings.title: isAccessTokenId() matcher has inverted logic and wrong substring offset, so it never actually validates the grant shortcut
findings.body: `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)` is supposed to assert that the 4th/5th characters of the encoded token-id context equal the expected grant-type shortcut (as the comment above states, chars 4-5, i.e. `substring(4, 6)`). Instead: (1) it uses `substring(3, 5)` which is the wrong character range (off-by-one, grabs the last char of the token-type shortcut plus the first char of the grant-type shortcut), and (2) the condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no match) precisely when the substring equals the expected value, and otherwise falls through to only check that the raw id portion is a UUID, effectively ignoring the grant-type shortcut entirely. This means `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken`, and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` (all of which rely on this matcher) will fail when the grant shortcut is actually correct, and will incorrectly pass when it is wrong, defeating the purpose of the added assertion and potentially causing spurious CI failures or false-positive test passes.

findings.title: New abstract method getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
findings.body: OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a public extension SPI (used to plug in custom OAuth2 grant types). This PR adds a new abstract method `String getShortcut();` with no default implementation. Any existing third-party/custom implementation of this SPI will fail to compile or fail provider loading until it implements this new method, which is a backward-incompatible API change for an SPI explicitly intended to be extensible (as mentioned in the PR description itself). A default method (e.g. returning a generated/fallback shortcut) would avoid breaking existing providers.

findings.title: getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut dereference sessionFactory without a null check, causing NPE instead of a clear error
findings.body: `getShortcutByGrantType()` (line 110) and `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` (line 125) use `sessionFactory` to refresh the shortcut maps when a lookup misses, but `sessionFactory` is only assigned in `postInit()`. If these methods are invoked on an instance where `postInit()` has not run (e.g. unusual initialization ordering, or direct instantiation as done in the accompanying unit test), a NullPointerException is thrown instead of the intended, user-facing `IllegalArgumentException`/`IllegalStateException` for unknown shortcuts/grant types. This makes failure diagnosis harder in edge cases and indicates the methods should defensively check for a null `sessionFactory`.

findings.title: testIncorrectGrantType masks a NullPointerException instead of verifying the intended error
findings.body: `testIncorrectGrantType()` never calls `factory.postInit(...)`, so `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.sessionFactory` remains null. When `getTokenContextFromTokenId("ofrtac:5678")` looks up the unknown shortcut "ac", `getGrantTypeByShortcut()` falls through to `sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...)`, which throws a NullPointerException rather than the intended `IllegalArgumentException` for 'Unknown value ... for grant type'. The test's `catch (RuntimeException iae)` is broad enough to swallow this NPE, so the test passes without actually verifying that unknown grant shortcuts produce the expected, well-formed error message; it only proves that *some* RuntimeException is thrown, which hides the underlying defect described separately in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.java.

findings.title: Access token 'jti' is no longer an opaque random UUID; no backward-compatibility note or opt-out
findings.body: `initToken()` now builds the access token id via `encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx)`, producing ids like `onrtac:1f65761e-...` instead of a plain UUID as before. External tooling, log parsers, audit systems, or custom code relying on the `jti` claim being a canonical UUID (fixed length/format) will break after upgrading. The PR introduces no migration notes, deprecation warning, or configuration flag to retain the previous plain-UUID behavior for users who depend on the old format, which is a user-facing behavioral/API change for a widely consumed token claim.

findings.title: Decoding logic unconditionally treats any colon-containing token id as encoded context, risking false failures for unrelated legacy ids
findings.body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` treats the presence of a ':' anywhere in the token id as indicating the new context-encoded format, then requires the prefix to be exactly 6 characters matching known shortcuts, throwing `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise. If any pre-existing or externally generated token id (not produced by this encoder) happens to contain a ':' for unrelated reasons, this method will throw a hard error instead of gracefully treating the whole string as a raw/legacy id (as is done for ids without a colon). This is a stricter contract than the previous 'any string is a valid token id' assumption, and has no fallback path for ids that incidentally contain a colon but aren't 6-char-shortcut encoded.
